title: Project Delivery Methods: Choosing Who Carries the Risk
summary: The delivery method decides who carries design, price and schedule risk on a building, and it is chosen before anyone digs. Each method buys one kind of certainty by giving up another, so the owner must decide which risks to keep before choosing.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the delivery method is the first risk decision on a building, and it is made before a single drawing is finished. No method gives price certainty, schedule certainty and design control at once; each one trades one of them for the others.

In plain English

A delivery method is the arrangement that says who designs the building, who builds it, when the price is fixed and who answers when something is wrong. The owner signs it, so the owner is choosing which problems will land on his desk. A good choice starts with a short written list: the risks you are willing to keep, and the risks you want someone else to carry and are prepared to pay them to carry.

Design-Bid-Build

The owner hires a designer, the designer completes the drawings, contractors bid on the finished set, and the lowest responsive bidder builds it. The strength is real price competition on a complete design. The weakness is sequence: nothing is built until design is finished, and the owner stands between the designer and the builder. Under the American doctrine that grew from the 1918 Supreme Court case United States v. Spearin, an owner who furnishes plans and specifications is generally taken to warrant that they are adequate. In practice that means a defect in the drawings is usually the owner's cost, not the contractor's. You recover it, if at all, from your designer.

Design-Build

One entity designs and builds under one contract. The owner gets a single point of responsibility, faster start because design and construction overlap, and often an early lump-sum price. The cost is independence: the designer now works for the builder, so the person who once checked the builder's interests on your behalf is on the other side of the table. Under Design-Build the owner's representative, an independent engineer or project manager reporting only to you, stops being optional. The owner also gives up much of his ability to direct the design after the brief is signed, so the brief, the performance requirements, carries the whole of the owner's intent.

Construction Manager at Risk

The owner hires the designer and, early, a construction manager who prices the design as it develops and later commits to a Guaranteed Maximum Price. The method suits a repetitive building, such as an apartment block with many identical floors, because construction pricing and buildability advice arrive while the design can still change cheaply. The Guaranteed Maximum Price is only as good as its definitions: the exclusions, the allowances, the contingency and who owns any unspent contingency at the end.

Integrated Project Delivery

A multi-party agreement in which owner, designer and builder share risk and reward against a target cost. It exists, it can work, and it is rare on small and mid-size work because it demands mature, trusting parties and specialist contracts.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical building with a construction estimate of 20 million in round units. Suppose the design is 40 percent complete when a Construction Manager at Risk offers a Guaranteed Maximum Price of 20 million, including a contractor's contingency of 600,000 and allowances of 1,000,000 for finishes not yet selected.

  1. Allowances are not prices. If the selected finishes cost 1,400,000, the 400,000 difference is usually added to the contract sum. Your certain price is really 19 million of firm work plus an estimate.
  2. Design at 40 percent means 60 percent of the information that fixes cost does not yet exist. Expect the price to be tested by scope arguments as the drawings develop; ask what percentage of design the price is based on, and treat anything below about 60 percent as a figure that will move.
  3. Ask who owns unspent contingency. If 300,000 of the 600,000 is unused and the contract returns it to the owner, that is 300,000 back. If the contract is silent or gives it to the contractor, it is profit. One sentence in the agreement decides a sum larger than many design fees.

Now compare a Design-Bid-Build route. Competitive bids on a complete set might land at 19.5 million, cheaper on paper, but design takes longer before construction starts. If the owner's carrying cost (interest and lost income) is 80,000 a month and the sequential route adds five months, the delay costs 400,000, which wipes out most of the bid saving. Delivery choice is a calculation, not a preference.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a method for the certainty it seems to offer without paying for the conditions that make it real. A lump sum on an incomplete brief is not certainty; it is a future claim. A Guaranteed Maximum Price without a written exclusions list is a ceiling with holes in it. And until real bids arrive against a real drawing set, any construction number you carry is an estimate, however confidently it is stated.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes a verbal assurance. A contractor, consultant or official who says "that will be fine" has committed to nothing that will survive a dispute. Every approval, every assumption and every exclusion goes in writing. The second mistake is dropping the independent reviewer to save a fee under Design-Build, at exactly the moment the owner loses his natural one.

How you will use it

Before choosing, write a one-page risk allocation: design adequacy, ground conditions, price escalation, schedule, and approvals, with a column for who should carry each. Then choose the method that puts most of them where you want them, and price the rest. Have construction counsel draft or review the agreement, and keep an owner's representative on your side of the table under any method. Professional sign-off required: construction counsel licensed in the project's jurisdiction.
checklist: Write down which risks you will keep and which you want transferred before choosing a method.
Keep an independent owner's representative reporting only to you, especially under Design-Build.
On any Guaranteed Maximum Price, get the exclusions, allowances and contingency definitions in writing.
Ask who owns unspent contingency at the end of the job.
Ask what percentage of design the price is based on; below about 60 percent expect movement.
Put every approval and assumption in writing; verbal assurances do not survive disputes.
Treat any number without real bids against a real drawing set as an estimate.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A builder offers you a lump-sum Design-Build price on a two-page brief and says it gives you full price certainty. What do you ask before believing it?
selftest.a: Ask what the price assumes about everything the brief does not say: finishes, ground conditions, performance standards, approvals and exclusions. A lump sum on an incomplete brief moves the argument from price to scope, so certainty only exists once the performance requirements are complete enough that a disagreement about scope can be settled by reading them. Also ask who will review the design on your behalf, because under Design-Build the designer works for the builder.

apply: Draft a one-page risk allocation table for a hypothetical building: list design, ground, price escalation, schedule and approvals, and mark who you would want to carry each one.
sources: Spearin doctrine: United States v. Spearin, 248 U.S. 132 (1918); how it applies varies by jurisdiction and contract wording. Delivery method descriptions follow common American industry usage (AIA, ConsensusDocs and DBIA document families); confirm the current editions and your jurisdiction with construction counsel. All figures are round hypothetical numbers.

title: The Contract Documents, and What Wins When They Contradict
summary: A construction contract is a stack of document types that together bind the parties, with drawings showing quantity and location and specifications showing quality and workmanship. When two documents genuinely conflict, an order-of-precedence clause decides, and without one ambiguity tends to fall on whoever drafted it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the contract is not one document; it is a stack, and anything in any layer of the stack binds. When two layers disagree, the precedence clause decides, so you read that clause before you sign rather than after the dispute.

In plain English

The documents for a building are designed to complement each other: the drawings show where things go and how much of them there is, the specifications say what they are made of and how they must be installed, and the agreement says who pays whom and when. Because they are complementary, a requirement shown only in the specification is still part of the contract even if no drawing shows it. Conflicts arise when two documents say different things about the same item, and then something has to decide which one wins.

The stack

A typical American set contains the agreement itself, the general conditions, any supplementary conditions, the drawings, the specifications, addenda issued during bidding, and modifications issued after signing. The general conditions usually come from a standard family such as AIA A201, ConsensusDocs or EJCDC; internationally FIDIC is common. Each family has its own wording and its own risk balance, so the choice of family is itself a negotiation.

The specification is organised by MasterFormat division, and each section follows three parts. Part 1, General, covers submittals, quality assurance, delivery and warranties. Part 2, Products, covers materials and acceptable manufacturers. Part 3, Execution, covers installation, tolerances, field testing and protection. Owners tend to read Part 2 because it names products. The money is in Parts 1 and 3, where submittals, tolerances and tests live.

Order of precedence

Well-drafted contracts include an express clause ranking the documents. A common pattern places modifications first, then the agreement, then supplementary and general conditions, then specifications, and drawings near the bottom, with larger-scale drawings over smaller-scale ones and figured dimensions over scaled ones. That is a pattern, not a rule; your contract's wording governs. Where no precedence clause exists, courts in many American jurisdictions apply the rule that ambiguity is construed against the party that drafted the document, which is usually the owner [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example

Suppose a structural drawing note calls for concrete of 4,000 psi in a ground slab, and the specification section calls for 3,500 psi. The difference on a hypothetical 300 cubic metre slab might be 10 per cubic metre, so 3,000 in material alone.

  1. Read the precedence clause. If specifications rank above drawings, 3,500 psi governs contractually.
  2. Do not stop there. Ask the structural engineer of record which strength the design actually requires. Contractual precedence decides who pays; it does not decide whether the slab is adequate.
  3. Resolve it in writing before award, by addendum, when it costs nothing. After award, the same correction is a change order priced by someone who knows you cannot shop it elsewhere.
  4. If the engineer confirms 4,000 psi, issue the addendum and make every bidder acknowledge it in writing.

The 3,000 is not the point. The point is that a two-minute check before bids closed would have turned a future claim into a line in an addendum.

Substitutions and equals

Specifications often name a product "or approved equal". Read who approves the equal. If the answer is the contractor, the contractor is approving his own cheaper substitute. The approver should be the design professional, on a written request with technical data, before purchase.

Addenda, modifications and the record

Two kinds of document change the stack after it is first drawn up. Addenda are issued during bidding and become part of every bid; modifications, which include change orders, construction change directives and written interpretations, are issued after signing and usually rank highest because they are the latest statement of intent. Both need a clean record. Keep a single document register listing every drawing and specification section, its current revision and the date it was issued, and make sure every party works from the same register. When a dispute arrives months later, the first question is always which revision was current on the day the work was done, and a register answers it in a minute.

The same discipline applies to written interpretations. When the architect or engineer answers an RFI by clarifying a drawing, that answer is a contract interpretation. File it against the drawing it clarifies, so that the next person who opens the drawing sees it. An interpretation that lives only in an email thread will be forgotten by the time the same detail is built on a later floor.

Finally, read the definitions article of the general conditions. Words such as "provide", "furnish", "install", "substantial completion" and "the Work" are usually defined there, and a single defined word can move a cost from one party to another. "Furnish" alone, for example, often means supply without installation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an incomplete list of contract documents. "The drawings" is not a list. If the agreement does not name every drawing and specification section by title, date and revision, the parties can later disagree about which revision was the contract, and the argument starts from nothing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the price and the schedule and skips the general conditions as boilerplate. The general conditions contain notice periods, payment terms, change procedures, claims and termination. A notice period missed by a week can forfeit a legitimate entitlement for either side. The other mistake is accepting an unacknowledged addendum: every bidder must confirm every addendum in writing, or the first dispute will be about whether he priced it.

How you will use it

Before signing, confirm the agreement lists every document by title, date and revision; confirm it has an express precedence clause and read it; read Parts 1 and 3 of the specification sections for structure, envelope and life safety; and make sure substitutions are approved by the designer. Have counsel confirm the general conditions family suits your jurisdiction. Professional sign-off required: construction counsel, and the architect and engineer of record for technical conflicts.
checklist: List every contract document in the agreement by title, date and revision number.
Confirm the contract has an express order-of-precedence clause and read it before signing.
Read Part 1 and Part 3 of specification sections for structure, envelope and life safety.
Make sure acceptable equals and substitutions are approved by the designer, not the contractor.
Have counsel confirm the general conditions family suits the jurisdiction.
Require every bidder to acknowledge every addendum in writing.
Resolve any drawing-versus-specification conflict in writing before award.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: After award, the contractor points out that the drawings show a waterproofing membrane on a wall that the specification does not mention, and asks for a change order. How do you approach it?
selftest.a: Start from the principle that the documents are complementary: something shown on the drawings is part of the contract even if the specification is silent, so the membrane may already be in the contract sum. Check the precedence clause only if the two documents genuinely conflict, which silence is not. Then read whether the specification section for waterproofing covers that wall by reference. Ask counsel before conceding, and in future close such gaps before bidding.

apply: Pick any standard form of general conditions you can access and find its order-of-precedence wording and its notice period for claims. Write both down in one sentence each.
sources: Document structure follows common American practice (AIA A201, ConsensusDocs, EJCDC; FIDIC internationally) and the CSI MasterFormat three-part section format; confirm current editions. The construction-against-the-drafter rule (contra proferentem) varies by jurisdiction [unverified — confirm independently]. Figures are hypothetical.

title: Submittals, RFIs and Long-Lead Items, and How Documents Destroy Buildings
summary: Shop drawings and submittals close the gap between design intent and what is fabricated, and long-lead items must be ordered by working backwards from the date they are needed. The Hyatt Regency and Citicorp Center cases show that a small detailing change can change how a structure carries load.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the design shows what is wanted; shop drawings show what will actually be made, and the gap between the two is where buildings are lost. Procurement fails silently, so you track it before you track construction progress.

In plain English

Before a fabricator cuts steel, bends reinforcement or orders a lift, he draws exactly what he will make and sends it to the design team as a submittal. The design team reviews it and stamps it with one of four common outcomes: no exceptions taken, reviewed as noted, revise and resubmit, or rejected. A question that cannot wait for a submittal travels as a Request for Information, an RFI. Both run on a clock, and both have to be tracked.

What a review stamp means

Design review of a submittal is typically for general conformance with the design intent only. The stamp language in most specifications says so expressly and leaves responsibility for dimensions, quantities and fabrication with the contractor. That language is correct and should stay in your specification, but understand what it means: the stamp is not a safety net, and the reviewer did not check every number.

The difference between "reviewed as noted" and "revise and resubmit" is often two to three weeks of schedule, because the second outcome restarts the cycle. Treat every resubmittal as a schedule event and ask, in the meeting, whether it touches the critical path.

Long-lead items

Some items take longer to procure than the building takes to reach them: lifts, switchgear, standby generators, fire pumps, curtain wall, specialist structural steel. They are ordered by working backwards from the date they are needed on site, through delivery, manufacture, submittal approval and design release. For imported equipment, the true lead time includes ocean freight, customs clearance and inland haul, not just the manufacturer's quoted weeks. Some items gate occupancy rather than construction, such as lifts and life safety systems, and those delay income, not merely the building.

A worked example

Suppose a lift is needed for installation in week 60 of a hypothetical programme. Work backwards in round weeks:

  1. Installation start: week 60. Allow 2 weeks of site storage and inspection before that: delivery by week 58.
  2. Freight, customs and inland haul: 8 weeks. Leaves the factory by week 50.
  3. Manufacture: 20 weeks. Order released by week 30.
  4. Submittal review including one resubmittal: 6 weeks. First submittal by week 24.
  5. Supplier's preparation of submittal: 4 weeks. Order must be placed, and design information released, by week 20.

If the design team cannot fix the lift shaft dimensions until week 26, the lift is already six weeks late before any concrete is poured. That is why the long-lead log is reviewed before the progress photographs.

The cases

Hyatt Regency, Kansas City, 1981. Suspended walkways in a hotel atrium collapsed during a crowded event and killed 114 people. As the public investigations describe it, the design called for continuous hanger rods from the roof through both walkways; during detailing this was changed to two shorter rods, so that the upper walkway's box beam connection carried both walkways. The change roughly doubled the load on that connection. The lesson for an owner is that a fabrication simplification can change a load path, and shop drawing review is the last line of defence.

Citicorp Center, New York, 1978. After completion, the structural engineer learned that welded joints in the wind bracing had been replaced with bolted joints, and that wind from certain diagonal directions governed more than had been checked. The connections were strengthened quietly and quickly. The lesson is that a field substitution can change how a tower responds to load, and that prompt disclosure when an error is found is the right response.

Both cases are summarised from public investigations and accounts; read the primary reports before quoting details.

RFIs as a measurement

An RFI log tells you about the health of the design. A steady trickle of questions is normal on any building. A flood of RFIs on one discipline, or many RFIs that the designer answers by issuing revised drawings, tells you that the drawings were issued before they were coordinated. Each RFI also carries a response time in the contract, often a stated number of working days, and every day your design team takes beyond it is exposure you carry, not the contractor. Track two numbers each month: how many RFIs are open, and how many are past their response date. If the second number grows, ask the design team for a recovery plan before the contractor asks for time.

Distinguish a genuine question from a disguised change. An RFI that asks "may we substitute this product" or "the drawing shows X, we propose Y" is a substitution request and should go through the substitution procedure, with technical data and the designer's written approval. Answering it casually by email is how a substitution reaches site without anyone checking its load path or its fire rating.

Finally, keep the four common review outcomes in mind when you read the register: an item marked no exceptions taken may proceed; reviewed as noted may proceed with the noted corrections; revise and resubmit may not proceed; rejected must start again. A fabricator who proceeds on a revise-and-resubmit is working at his own risk, and the register should show it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a substitution or "constructability improvement" to a structural element that reaches site without the engineer of record answering one question: does this change the load path? Four other failure modes cost money rather than lives: scope gaps at trade boundaries, clashes between disciplines, drawing-versus-specification conflicts, and ground conditions the investigation did not anticipate.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner watches the site, which looks busy, and ignores procurement, which fails silently. The second mistake is accepting a verbal "the engineer is fine with it" for a structural change.

How you will use it

Demand a submittal register (item, owner, date required, date submitted, date returned, outcome) and a separate long-lead log with an order-by date for each item. Review the log first at every meeting. Require structural substitutions to go to the engineer of record in writing with an explicit load-path question, and require written confirmation that connection shop drawings were checked against design assumptions. Require clash detection before drawings are issued for construction. Make reporting a possible error safe; you set that by how you react the first time. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record.
checklist: Demand a submittal register with dates required, submitted, returned and outcome.
Keep a separate long-lead log with an order-by date derived backwards from need.
Treat every revise-and-resubmit as a schedule event and ask about the critical path.
Use delivered-to-site dates for imported equipment, with freight and customs shown separately.
Send every structural substitution to the engineer of record in writing with a load-path question.
Require clash detection before drawings are issued for construction.
Make reporting a possible error safe and expected.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A fabricator proposes replacing one long continuous hanger rod with two shorter rods because the long rod is hard to thread. The superintendent says it is a minor detailing change. What do you do?
selftest.a: Stop it until the structural engineer of record has answered in writing whether the change alters the load path and the load on each connection. This is the Hyatt Regency pattern: splitting a continuous rod can make one connection carry the load of more than one level. A detailing change to a structural element is never minor until the engineer has checked it.

apply: Build a backwards procurement timeline for one hypothetical imported item, showing need date, delivery, freight, manufacture, review and order date in weeks.
sources: Hyatt Regency (1981) and Citicorp Center (1978) are summarised from public investigation reports and published accounts; read the primary reports (including the National Bureau of Standards investigation of the Hyatt walkways) before quoting details. Submittal stamp practice follows common American specification language. Figures are hypothetical.

title: Change Orders, Markup, and the Clauses You Fix Before You Sign
summary: Changes come from the owner, from design errors and omissions, and from differing site conditions, and two of the three are usually the owner's cost. Markup, unit rates, notice and the critical-path test for time are fixed before signing, because the owner's leverage drops sharply the day after.
body:
Mr Shabazz, most change order disputes are won or lost before the contract is signed, in the clauses that decide how a change is priced. After signature you are negotiating with someone who knows you cannot take the work elsewhere.

In plain English

A change order adjusts the contract: more work, less work, different work, or more time. Changes come from three places: the owner changing his mind, errors and omissions in the design, and site conditions that differ from what the documents described. The first is plainly yours. The second is usually yours against the contractor, recoverable if at all from the designer. The third depends on the contract, as a later lesson shows. So most changes cost the owner, and the only question is how much.

The four parts of a change order

Every priced change has direct cost (labour, material and plant, with quantities and unit rates), subcontractor cost, markup for overhead and profit, and any time extension. The first three you can check; the markup you should already have fixed. If the contract is silent on markup, it will be argued separately on every change, and the contractor will propose a number that suits him.

Cost and time are separate entitlements

A change can cost money without adding time, and only a change that delays the critical path, the longest chain of dependent activities that sets the finish date, entitles the contractor to more time. A baseline schedule showing the critical path, submitted soon after award and updated monthly, is the tool that lets you answer that question. Without it, every time claim becomes an argument.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical change adds 40 square metres of block wall. The contractor's direct cost is labour 2,400, material 1,600 and plant 400, so 4,400.

  1. With markup fixed in the contract at 10 percent on self-performed work: 4,400 times 1.10 is 4,840.
  2. With markup unfixed, the contractor proposes 20 percent overhead plus 10 percent profit, compounded: 4,400 times 1.20 times 1.10 is 5,808. One change, nearly 1,000 more.
  3. Across 80 similar changes over the job, that difference is about 77,000, from one unwritten sentence.
  4. Now suppose an agreed unit rate for block wall was fixed at award: 115 per square metre including markup. The change prices itself at 40 times 115, which is 4,600, and nobody argues.

Next, time. If the wall is in a stair core on the critical path and takes three days, the contractor may be entitled to three days. If it is in a ground-floor storeroom with twenty days of float, the cost is due and the time is not.

Liquidated damages

Liquidated damages are a pre-agreed daily sum the contractor pays for late completion. They should be a genuine pre-estimate of the owner's loss, typically lost income plus finance cost, not a penalty; enforceability depends on the jurisdiction and on that being so [unverified — confirm independently]. Suppose interest costs the owner 2,000 a day and lost rent 3,000 a day; a rate near 5,000 a day is defensible, and the calculation should be kept on file.

Retention and lien law

Retention is money held back from each payment until completion. Many jurisdictions also have statutory holdback or lien rules that apply whatever the contract says. Do not assume the rules of one place apply in another; have counsel confirm them [unverified — confirm independently].

Where changes come from, and how to limit them

The cheapest change is the one that never happens. Owner changes are reduced by freezing decisions on a schedule: finishes, layouts and equipment choices each get a decision date, and a choice made after its date is priced as a change on purpose, so everyone feels the cost. Design changes are reduced by coordination before issue, which is why clash detection and an independent constructability review are worth their fees. Site-condition changes are reduced by investigation, which is the subject of Week Three.

Distinguish three instruments. A change order is agreed by both parties on price and time. A construction change directive lets the owner instruct the work to proceed while price is still being agreed, so that the site does not stop while two parties argue; it should then be priced on the agreed basis, usually cost plus the fixed markup. A minor change in the work, with no cost or time effect, can be instructed by the designer. Using a directive keeps the job moving, but it should be the exception, because an unpriced directive is an open cheque until it is settled. Track open directives as a number on every report.

Finally, keep a change log with the running total of approved and pending changes against the contingency. When pending changes plus approved changes approach the contingency, the owner needs to know before the money is spent, not after.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approving a change verbally. A verbal instruction becomes a claim later at whatever price the contractor then chooses, with no record of what was agreed. A written instruction takes ten minutes, and the discipline is the whole point.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner negotiates the contract sum down by two percent and signs a contract silent on markup, unit rates and change procedure. On a job with many changes, the two percent comes back through the changes, often with interest. Your leverage peaks the day before signature; spend it on the clauses, not only on the headline number.

How you will use it

Before signing, fix markup percentages separately for self-performed and subcontracted work; negotiate unit rates at award for repetitive elements; require full breakdowns with quantities and rates and reject lump sums; require a critical-path baseline schedule before the first payment; and keep the liquidated damages calculation on file. For every change, ask two questions on the record: what does it cost, and does it touch the critical path. Professional sign-off required: construction counsel for liquidated damages, retention and lien provisions; cost consultant for unit rates.
checklist: Never approve a change verbally; issue a written instruction every time.
Require a full cost breakdown with quantities and unit rates; reject lump-sum change prices.
Fix markup in the contract, separately for self-performed and subcontracted work.
Agree unit rates at award for repetitive elements so most changes price themselves.
Require a critical-path baseline schedule before the first payment.
Ask of every change what it costs and whether it touches the critical path.
Calculate liquidated damages from real exposure and keep the calculation on file.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A contractor submits a change order with a single lump sum of 25,000 and a request for ten extra days, for work in an area with substantial float. How do you respond?
selftest.a: Reject the lump sum and ask for a breakdown of labour, material, plant and subcontract costs with quantities and rates, then apply the contractually fixed markup. On time, ask for the schedule analysis showing the change delays the critical path; if the work sits in an area with float, the cost may be due but the time extension is not.

apply: Write two contract sentences for a hypothetical building: one fixing markup on changes, and one stating how a time extension must be demonstrated against the critical path.
sources: Change order structure and markup practice reflect common American contract forms (AIA A201, ConsensusDocs). Liquidated damages enforceability, retention and statutory lien or holdback rules vary by jurisdiction [unverified — confirm independently]. All figures are hypothetical; markup percentages are commercial practice, not law.

title: Week One Review: Delivery, Documents, Submittals and Changes
summary: Six scenario questions covering delivery methods, contract precedence, submittals and long-lead items, and change orders, each with a worked answer. The week's thread is that the owner's risk is mostly fixed on paper before any work starts.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week was about decisions made on paper before the site opens. Answer each question aloud before you read the answer; the reasoning matters more than the words.

Question 1. You are planning a repetitive apartment building and want reliable construction cost information early, while the design can still change. Which delivery method fits, and what risk comes with it?

Answer. Construction Manager at Risk fits, because a construction manager prices the design as it develops and later commits to a Guaranteed Maximum Price, and a repetitive building rewards early buildability advice. The risk is in the definitions behind the guaranteed price: exclusions, allowances, contingency and who owns unspent contingency. A price based on a design well below about 60 percent complete will move. Keep an independent owner's representative on your side throughout.

Question 2. A drawing note calls for one concrete strength and the specification calls for another. Which governs, and what do you actually do?

Answer. The contract's order-of-precedence clause decides which governs contractually; in many contracts specifications rank above drawings, but your wording rules. Then ask the structural engineer of record which strength the design requires, because precedence decides who pays, not whether the slab is adequate. Resolve it by addendum before award, when it costs nothing, and require every bidder to acknowledge the addendum in writing.

Question 3. A slab measures 30 metres by 20 metres by 0.25 metres. What is its theoretical volume, and how much do you order at five percent waste?

Answer. Theoretical volume is 30 times 20 times 0.25, which is 150 cubic metres. Five percent waste is 7.5 cubic metres, so 157.5, rounded up to 158 cubic metres. At 8 cubic metres a truck that is 20 loads, which you check against the supplier's real truck capacity and pump rate before pour day. The quantity takeoff that sits behind this arithmetic is next week's first lesson.

Question 4. A reinforcement submittal comes back marked revise and resubmit, and you are told this is routine. Is it?

Answer. It is common, but it is not neutral. A resubmittal restarts the review cycle and typically costs two to three weeks. Ask in the meeting whether the reinforcement for that element sits on the critical path and what the resubmittal does to the date it is needed. Record the answer. A submittal register with required and returned dates makes this visible before it becomes a delay.

Question 5. On site, a fabricator proposes splitting one continuous hanger rod that supports two walkway levels into two shorter rods, because threading the long rod is difficult. The superintendent says yes. What do you say?

Answer. Stop it until the structural engineer of record confirms in writing whether the change alters the load path. This is the Hyatt Regency pattern: with two rods, the upper connection carries both levels, roughly doubling its load. A fabrication convenience on a structural element is a design change, and the stamp on a shop drawing is not a guarantee that someone checked it.

Question 6. Your draft contract is silent on change order markup, but you have negotiated two percent off the contract sum. Do you sign?

Answer. Not yet. Fix markup percentages for self-performed and subcontracted work, agree unit rates for repetitive elements, require full breakdowns, and require a critical-path baseline schedule. On a job with many changes, unfixed markup can return the two percent and more. Your leverage is highest the day before signature; spend it on the clauses.

Recap

The delivery method decides who carries design, price and schedule risk, and no method gives all three certainties at once. Under Design-Bid-Build the owner generally warrants the design he furnishes, under the American Spearin doctrine. Under Design-Build the owner gains one point of responsibility and loses his independent reviewer, so he must hire one back. Construction Manager at Risk suits repetitive buildings when its guaranteed price is properly defined.

The contract is a stack of complementary documents, and precedence decides genuine conflicts. Read Parts 1 and 3 of the specification sections that govern structure, envelope and life safety, and make sure substitutions are approved by the designer. List every document by title, date and revision.

Submittals translate design into fabrication. Review stamps are for general conformance, not a guarantee. Long-lead items are ordered backwards from need, with freight and customs included for imported equipment, and the long-lead log is reviewed before the progress photographs. Hyatt Regency and Citicorp Center show that a detailing change can change a load path.

Changes come from the owner, design errors and site conditions, and most land on the owner. Fix markup and unit rates before signing, require breakdowns, separate cost from time, and test time against the critical path. Never approve a change verbally.

The thread: the owner's real risk on a building is mostly decided on paper, before any work starts, by documents most owners skim. Read them while your leverage is highest. Professional sign-off required: construction counsel for the agreement and general conditions; structural engineer of record for any structural change.

One habit links all four lessons. Each time a document, a submittal or a change crosses your desk, ask two questions: who carries the risk if this is wrong, and is that written down? If you cannot answer both, the risk is yours by default.

Next week moves from paper to quantities and time: the takeoff behind a price, the programme behind a date, the logistics behind the programme, and the survey behind every level on the drawings.
checklist: Match the delivery method to the risks you want to keep and transfer.
Read the precedence clause and resolve conflicts before award.
Check concrete volumes yourself and confirm truck and pump capacity with the supplier.
Treat every resubmittal as a possible critical-path event.
Send every structural detailing change to the engineer of record in writing.
Fix markup and unit rates before signing the contract.

selftest.q: Which single document would you review first at a project meeting to detect a delay that the site does not yet show?
selftest.a: The long-lead procurement log, with order-by dates derived backwards from need. Procurement fails silently while the site still looks busy, so a missed order date shows up there weeks or months before it shows up as an idle crew.
